card.hook: The Star of India is so long that she keeps sliding out of your photo, like a cat that won't sit still. Three tall masts, a dark iron hull and the whole San Diego waterfront behind her, and you want every bit of it in one frame.
card.stand_here: Stand on the North Harbor Drive sidewalk, on the landside facing the ship, roughly at Ash Street. The ship lies to the west of you, so face west. From here the whole hull and all three masts fit in one picture.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for the full ship. If you can't get far enough back, switch to 0.5x, but keep her in the middle of the frame so the masts don't lean. Then try zoom 2x to 5x (depends on your phone) for the figurehead, the captain's wheel and the rigging.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and line the masts up with the vertical lines, then tap the ship's hull and slide the brightness down a little so the sky keeps its colour and the dark hull doesn't wash out.
card.best_time: Morning on a sunny day is what one guide recommends for shooting from the landside. If you're still around at sunset, the Embarcadero is a lovely second stop, with the ship in the foreground and the bay glowing behind her.
card.selfie_here: Head to the Embarcadero promenade by the Star of India, on North Harbor Drive near Ash Street. Use the front camera, try 0.5x, and see if you can get the ship over your shoulder (check the angle on your screen). At sunset you may also catch the glow on the water and the Point Loma lights in the distance.
card.rules_and_safety: Personal photography is welcome aboard the ship, but commercial photography needs permission. Going aboard needs a museum ticket (check the official site first), while the waterfront sidewalk view is free. If you go aboard, wear closed-toe, rubber-soled shoes, because of the steep ladders, hatches and sloped decks.
card.challenge: Get all three masts standing perfectly straight against the gridlines, with a little sky left above the tallest one. Then walk closer and hunt down the figurehead at the bow.
card.good_to_know: The Star of India was built in 1863 on the Isle of Man, under the name Euterpe. Her iron hull has survived almost unchanged since then. She's now part of the Maritime Museum of San Diego and is said to be the oldest ship in the world that still sails regularly.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on the North Harbor Drive sidewalk, on the landside facing the ship, roughly at Ash Street. The ship lies to the west of you, so face west. From here the whole hull and all three masts fit in one picture.

card.hook: Most zoo photos are close-ups of one animal's face. The Skyfari flips that: you float over the treetops and the whole zoo spreads out below you like a leafy map.
card.stand_here: Stand right at the subject: the Skyfari east terminal on the eastern side of the zoo grounds, where you board. Once the tram sets off across the zoo, face outwards and down over the planted habitats, with Balboa Park beyond.
card.zoom: Start at 0.5x for the big sweep of treetops and habitats, then go to 1x for a more natural view. Try 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) to pick out an animal or the park beyond.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines, put the horizon on the upper third line and let the canopy fill the rest, with a few treetops in the foreground to show how high you are.
card.best_time: Pick a clear day so you can see across Balboa Park, and maybe even the downtown skyline far off. Mornings and late afternoons usually give softer light than midday.
card.selfie_here: Try the bamboo groves on the zoo grounds, with the foliage around you. Use the front camera and hold it a little above eye level. It's a fallback spot, so don't expect a big landmark behind you. The lush pool in the hippo habitat is another one to try for a watery backdrop.
card.rules_and_safety: Keep your arms and your phone inside the tram at all times. Selfie sticks aren't allowed in the zoo's wildlife habitat areas, and photos should be for personal use.
card.challenge: Take three frames at different moments of the ride and see which one makes the zoo look most like a jungle.
card.good_to_know: The zoo sits inside Balboa Park and grew out of animals left over from the 1915 Panama–California Exposition. Today it covers about 100 acres and has more than 12,000 animals of over 680 species and subspecies. The Skyfari was built in 1969 and needs zoo admission, so check the official site before you go for tickets and opening times.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand right at the subject: the Skyfari east terminal on the eastern side of the zoo grounds, where you board. Once the tram sets off across the zoo, face outwards and down over the planted habitats, with Balboa Park beyond.

card.hook: The Del looks like a wedding cake that got a bit carried away: white wooden walls, red turrets and a roofline with a lot to say. Spot it rising over the dunes and you'll know why everyone stops to take the picture.
card.stand_here: Head for the public sand just past the Hot Coal Bins line, right at the subject, and face north-west toward the hotel. You'll see the red turrets and roofline rising over the dunes and ice plant, with the ocean and sky filling the lower frame.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the whole width of the building, then go to 1x for a natural view. Try 2x to 5x to pick out a single turret or the roof details.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines, tap the building, then slide the brightness down a little so the sky keeps its colour and the roofs don't wash out.
card.best_time: Go in late afternoon or at sunset, when the light hits the ocean side of the hotel and turns the white walls pink.
card.selfie_here: Start where the sidewalk meets the walkway to the hotel on Ocean Boulevard, walk about 50 yards onto the sand and face north. Use the front camera with the red turrets behind you and the beach in the frame; late in the day the warm light brings out the red roofline.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the sand at Lifeguard Tower 2C, near the Avenida del Sol cul-de-sac, while you pose with the hotel in the background.
card.rules_and_safety: Take your photos from the public beach or the sidewalks. The hotel grounds are private property and have photography restrictions, so check the hotel's official site before you go.
card.challenge: Can you get a turret in the top corner of the frame with a little dune grass in front to give it depth, and keep the horizon level on the gridline?
card.good_to_know: The Hotel del Coronado, often just called The Del, opened in 1888, when it was the largest resort hotel in the world. It's a National Historic Landmark and is described as the second-largest wooden building in the United States.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Head for the public sand just past the Hot Coal Bins line, right at the subject, and face north-west toward the hotel. You'll see the red turrets and roofline rising over the dunes and ice plant, with the ocean and sky filling the lower frame.

card.hook: Picture a baseball stadium with a commuter train sliding along right below your feet. That's the Harbor Drive Pedestrian Bridge, and it gives you the whole Petco Park-meets-downtown scene in one tidy shot.
card.stand_here: Stand on the Harbor Drive Pedestrian Bridge, over the trolley tracks, and face north. The stadium is ahead of you with the downtown skyline rising behind it.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the stadium, the tracks and the skyline into one frame, and keep your phone level so the buildings stay straight. Want a calmer look with less stretching at the edges? Switch to 1x. Zoom 2x-5x (depending on your phone) is good for the brick warehouse or a passing train.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the stadium, then slide it a little darker if the sky is bright, so the brick and buildings keep their colour.
card.best_time: Early morning is likely to be quieter on the bridge, and you can expect more people around game times. Around dusk, switch on night mode for the lights and rest your elbows on the rail to keep the shot sharp.
card.selfie_here: Try the bridge walkway as you approach the stadium from the Gaslamp side. One blog says you can get a good shot with the park in the background while crossing, so the stadium sits behind you. Use the front camera, hold it a little low and keep the ballpark over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand further along the bridge while you stand in front of the stadium, so the whole ballpark fits behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: Selfie sticks aren't allowed at Petco Park, so ask a fellow fan for a photo. Access to the ballpark and viewing areas like Park at the Park can change on game days, so check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Turn on gridlines, line the tracks up with a horizontal line, then wait for a train to slide into the bottom of your frame. Try a Live Photo or a quick burst to catch it.
card.good_to_know: Petco Park is home to the San Diego Padres and opened in 2004. It sits at the edge of downtown, next to the Gaslamp Quarter. A historic brick warehouse, the Western Metal Supply Co. building, was built into the ballpark, and its corner is now the left field foul pole.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on the Harbor Drive Pedestrian Bridge, over the trolley tracks, and face north. The stadium is ahead of you with the downtown skyline rising behind it.

card.hook: Picture a calm pond, a leafy building with a fancy facade behind it, and a whole lot of sky. That's the Lily Pond view in Balboa Park, and it's the park's most photographed scene for good reason.
card.stand_here: Stand at the water's edge in front of the Botanical Building, across the Lily Pond, and face the building. Keep it centred so both sides of the facade look balanced.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to get the pond, the building and its reflection all in one go. Try 0.5x if the pond edge feels tight or the crowd is in the way, and 2x for close-ups of the facade and plants.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines, put the building on the centre line, and let the pond fill the lower third of the frame.
card.best_time: Early morning or sunset, when one photo guide says the reflections on the water can look good. Weekends and holidays get busy, so go early if you want the pond to yourself.
card.selfie_here: Head to the small fountain inside Alcazar Garden, where the California Tower is clearly in view. Use the front camera at 0.5x and put the tower over your shoulder. Cabrillo Bridge works too, with the skyline and the tower ahead.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand back from the front of the California Tower (Museum of Us) so the whole building fits, while you stand in front of it.
card.rules_and_safety: The park is an open public space, but the Botanical Building's interior has been closed at times, and some attractions, like the Museum of Us tower tour, are paid. Check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Get the building and its reflection in one shot with no ripples, then add a second photo with you crouched low at the water's edge.
card.good_to_know: Balboa Park covers about 1,200 acres and has been set aside for public recreation since 1835. The Botanical Building was designed by Carleton Winslow for the 1915 exposition, and back then it was the largest wood lath structure in the world. The park and its historic exposition buildings became a National Historic Landmark District in 1977.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand at the water's edge in front of the Botanical Building, across the Lily Pond, and face the building. Keep it centred so both sides of the facade look balanced.

card.hook: Fair warning: the Midway is a real aircraft carrier, and it's so big that getting all of it in one photo is half the fun. Its long grey hull, the planes parked on deck and the downtown skyline behind make a great waterfront picture.
card.stand_here: Stand in Tuna Harbor Park, just south of the carrier, and face north so you're looking at the ship's broadside with the city behind it. From the Embarcadero waterfront it's about 2 minutes on foot to the ship's pier. Put the Unconditional Surrender statue low in front of you.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for the side-on view. If the ship won't fit, drop to zoom 0.5x. Then try zoom 2x to 5x (depends on your phone) to pick out planes and details on the flight deck.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines to keep the long hull level, then tap the grey hull and slide darker a touch so the sky keeps its colour.
card.best_time: Go early in the morning, when the light on the ship's side is clean. Give yourself a few minutes at your spot to get one wide shot and one closer shot of the deck.
card.selfie_here: Take your selfie on the plaza beside the Unconditional Surrender statue in Tuna Harbor Park, turning so the ship is behind you. It's a popular photo op just steps from the Midway. Use the front camera and zoom 0.5x to fit more of the carrier in. For a close selfie with the hull behind you, try Broadway Pier, directly across from the museum.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by on the waterfront walkway beside North Harbor Drive to step back until the full length of the carrier fits in the shot behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: The waterfront around the ship is public space, but going aboard is a ticketed visit, so check the official site before you go. Also check for any closures around the Embarcadero.
card.challenge: Get the statue low in the frame with the whole carrier looming behind it, so the ship looks as huge as it really is.
card.good_to_know: Midway was the longest-serving US aircraft carrier of the 20th century, in service from 1945 to 1992. It opened to visitors as a museum on 7 June 2004. If you go aboard, you can climb into aircraft and cockpits, and scenes from Top Gun: Maverick were filmed here in 2018 and 2019.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand in Tuna Harbor Park, just south of the carrier, and face north so you're looking at the ship's broadside with the city behind it. From the Embarcadero waterfront it's about 2 minutes on foot to the ship's pier. Put the Unconditional Surrender statue low in front of you.

card.hook: Fifth Avenue is loud, bright and packed, and the prettiest building nearby is the calm one across the street. It's a Moorish and Spanish-style front, and it's one of the most photographed in the district.
card.stand_here: Stand at Balboa Theatre, on the sidewalk across from the front facade. Face the theatre so the whole front is in view, away from the main Fifth Avenue crowds.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the whole theatre front in from across the street, but keep important stuff away from the edges, where it can stretch. Then switch to 1x for a more natural look, and try 2x for details on the facade.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines, line the building's straight edges up with them, and keep the phone upright (not tilted back) so the facade doesn't lean.
card.best_time: Early morning is quieter, so you get cleaner shots with fewer people in the frame. In the evening the signs and lamps light up, so try night mode and steady the phone against a wall or post.
card.selfie_here: Head to the Gaslamp Quarter sign on the sidewalk at the corner of 5th Avenue and L Street and stand with the sign behind you. Use the front camera and zoom 0.5x if you want the whole sign over your shoulder. It's lit up after sunset, so it works by day or night.
card.ask_someone: At Horton Plaza Park, ask a passer-by to stand east of the fountain and shoot toward Broadway, while you stand in front of the fountain so it and the plaza fill the frame.
card.rules_and_safety: Stick to well-lit, populated streets and keep an eye on your belongings. One review said the Horton Plaza fountain was blocked off for construction, so check it's open before you go. If you want to go inside the theatre or any other building, check the official site first.
card.challenge: Get the theatre's front perfectly straight against your gridlines, then walk down the block and find one Victorian shopfront with a detail you'd never have spotted from a car.
card.good_to_know: Alonzo Horton began developing this part of town in 1867 and chose Fifth Avenue as its main street. Most of the area's 90-odd historic buildings date from the Victorian era. The district was renamed 'Gaslamp Quarter' during the 1980s restoration, and the arched sign over Fifth Avenue went up in 1992.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand at Balboa Theatre, on the sidewalk across from the front facade. Face the theatre so the whole front is in view, away from the main Fifth Avenue crowds.

card.hook: Picture whitewashed adobe walls, wooden verandas and an open courtyard, with not a single shopfront sneaking into the frame. That's the Casa de Estudillo courtyard, and it's the one picture to get here.
card.stand_here: Walk into the courtyard of Casa de Estudillo, inside the park, and turn to face the adobe walls. The park's mapped centre is to the north-west of the Old Town neighbourhood, about 1 minute on foot.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the walls, veranda and courtyard in together. Then go to 1x for a more natural look, and try 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) for doorways, beams and whitewashed corners.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the brightest part of the whitewashed wall, then slide the brightness down a little so the white keeps its texture and the shady verandas stay readable.
card.best_time: Go early in the morning. Guides say the park gets busy by midday at weekends, and many shops open late, so the courtyard is calmer first thing.
card.selfie_here: Use the front camera in the Casa de Estudillo courtyard, which one guide calls the most photogenic single spot in the park. Keep the adobe walls over your shoulder, and try 0.5x if you want more of the house in the shot. For a bolder backdrop, the colourful Fiesta de Reyes courtyard in the market area has papel picado and tile.
card.rules_and_safety: Wear comfortable shoes, because the park has cobblestone, dirt paths and some uneven sections. Elaborate photo setups need advance permission from the park superintendent.
card.challenge: Find a veranda post or doorway and tuck it into one edge of your frame, so the courtyard looks like it's peeking round the corner.
card.good_to_know: This was the heart of San Diego from 1820 to 1870, and five of the buildings here are original adobes. Casa de Estudillo was built in 1827 and is a National Historic Landmark in its own right. The park itself was established in 1968.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Walk into the courtyard of Casa de Estudillo, inside the park, and turn to face the adobe walls. The park's mapped centre is to the north-west of the Old Town neighbourhood, about 1 minute on foot.

card.hook: Picture a shopping centre where the streets are replaced by winding boardwalks, and the shopfronts jump from Victorian to traditional Mexican as you stroll. That's Seaport Village, and you can shoot it at a wander.
card.stand_here: Stand in Embarcadero Marina Park, on the yacht basin edge beside Seaport Village (the village itself lies to the north-west). Face across the boats towards the Grand Hyatt and Marriott towers.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the marina and skyline in. Switch to 1x for the carousel and shopfronts, then try 2x-5x (depending on your phone) to pick out the tower tops or a single boat.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on your gridlines, put the water's edge on a lower line, and let a few boats sit in the foreground so the picture has depth.
card.best_time: Late afternoon into dusk usually suits the marina view, and it's when the village's string lights come out. Mornings are generally quieter if you want clear shots of the paths.
card.selfie_here: Head to the front of the carousel building at 857 W. Harbor Dr. and stand beside the Looff tribute on the side of the building. Use the front camera and keep the carousel behind you, since it's the village's most-photographed feature.
card.rules_and_safety: Shops, rides and attractions can have their own rules, and the carousel's status can change, so check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Take one wide marina shot first, then walk in and catch the carousel with its string lights and a bit of bay behind it.
card.good_to_know: Seaport Village was built on landfill and opened in 1980. It has more than 70 shops, galleries and eateries. Its working carousel, with hand-carved animals, was built in 1895.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand in Embarcadero Marina Park, on the yacht basin edge beside Seaport Village (the village itself lies to the north-west). Face across the boats towards the Grand Hyatt and Marriott towers.

card.hook: Most bridges just get you across. This one swoops, and from the Coronado shore the whole curve arches over the downtown skyline like it was built for your photo.
card.stand_here: Stand in Coronado Tidelands Park, on the bayfront promenade under the east end of the bridge. On the map the bridge is to the south-east of this point. Face across the bay toward the downtown skyline, with the curve arching overhead.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the whole curve and the skyline in one frame. Try 1x for a calmer, more natural view. Then try 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) to pick out the city buildings under the arch.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines, line the skyline up with a horizontal line so the city doesn't lean, then tap the skyline and slide it a little darker so the sky keeps its colour.
card.best_time: Sunrise gives soft side-light and a near-empty park. Blue hour is best for the bridge and the city lights, so switch on night mode and tuck your elbows into your body to keep the phone steady.
card.selfie_here: Try the Coronado Bridge Viewpoint on the Silver Strand Bikeway, on the small sandy beach section among the palm trees, facing the bridge head-on. Use the front camera (or 0.5x if your phone offers it) and let the span rise over your shoulder. For colour instead, stand in front of the mural-covered pillars at Chicano Park.
card.ask_someone: At Cesar Chavez Park Public Pier 16, ask a passer-by to stand at the far end of the pier so they can frame the full arc of the bridge across the bay.
card.rules_and_safety: You can't walk on the bridge, and it isn't open to pedestrians or cyclists, so every good view is from the shoreline or below. Drone rules apply near it, so check the current rules and that the park and pier are open before you go.
card.challenge: Find the gap where the bridge's curve sits right above the buildings, then take one shot where the skyline is perfectly level. No leaning towers allowed!
card.good_to_know: The bridge opened on 3 August 1969, during San Diego's 200th anniversary celebrations. It's about 3.4 km (2.1 miles) long. The curve is there for a practical reason: the Navy wanted at least 61 m (200 feet) of clearance for ships, and bending the route let the road climb gently enough to reach that height.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand in Coronado Tidelands Park, on the bayfront promenade under the east end of the bridge. On the map the bridge is to the south-east of this point. Face across the bay toward the downtown skyline, with the curve arching overhead.

card.hook: Here's a lighthouse that was built so high it kept vanishing into the clouds. The Old Point Loma Lighthouse is a whitewashed tower with a black lantern room, and on a clear day it stands out beautifully.
card.stand_here: Stand at the Old Point Loma Lighthouse, on its east-facing entrance side, and face the tower. The white walls pop against the sky or the ocean, and a nearby cypress can sit to one side like a natural frame.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the whole lighthouse against the sky. Switch to 1x for the skyline and bay from the overlooks, then try 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) to pick out Coronado, boats or the lantern room.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the lighthouse wall, then drag the slider down a touch to make it slightly darker so the white walls keep their detail against a bright sky.
card.best_time: Go in the morning, when the sun lights up the east-facing entrance side. Fog and low cloud can drift in, so peek at the sky before you set out.
card.selfie_here: Try the flower-lined grounds beside the lighthouse, where the spring wildflowers grow, and use the front camera with the tower behind you. The Cabrillo statue viewing area also works: face the bay and you'll get a partial view of the lighthouse over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask someone to stand back on the flower-lined walkway below the lighthouse so the whole tower fits in the frame, while you pose up by the tower.
card.rules_and_safety: Small-scale still photography with hand-carried gear needs no permit if it's eight people or fewer in areas open to the public. Drones are prohibited. The lighthouse staircase is steep, narrow and circular, so take care on it. Check the official site before you go for entry and opening arrangements.
card.challenge: Take one shot of the lighthouse with the tower standing perfectly straight on the gridlines, then one where the cypress frames it. Which one wins?
card.good_to_know: Cabrillo National Monument marks Juan Rodríguez Cabrillo's landing at San Diego Bay on 28 September 1542. The lighthouse has stood on the park's highest point since 1855, 129 metres (422 feet) above sea level, and was closed in 1891 because fog and low cloud often hid its light. The Cabrillo statue is a limestone replica from 1988, because the 1949 sandstone original weathered badly.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand at the Old Point Loma Lighthouse, on its east-facing entrance side, and face the tower. The white walls pop against the sky or the ocean, and a nearby cypress can sit to one side like a natural frame.

card.hook: Most train stations are places you rush through, but this one has twin domes and a row of arches that make you stop mid-stride. Better still, there's nearly always a train or trolley rolling through.
card.stand_here: Stand at the corner of Kettner Boulevard and Broadway, by the fountain in front of the depot. Face the building across the open forecourt for a low, street-level view with the fountain beside you.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to fit the façade and fountain together. If the building won't fit from the corner, tap 0.5x, and use 2x or more (depending on your phone) to pick out the domes and tile detail.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and line them up with the building's vertical edges so the station doesn't lean, then keep the fountain low in the frame and let the domes fill the top.
card.best_time: Soft morning or late-afternoon light is worth a try on the plaster and tiles. Trains and trolleys pass at any hour, so there's always something moving in the shot.
card.selfie_here: Head into the forecourt plaza by the fountain and sit on or beside the tiled benches, with the station wall behind you. Use the front camera, hold it a little low, and switch to 0.5x if you want the domes and arches over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand in the plaza near the fountain and shoot back toward the south face of the depot, while you stand in front of the building so it fits in the frame.
card.rules_and_safety: This is a working station, so stay clear of doorways and platforms and don't block passengers. Check the official site for access changes or building work, and have a look at the current state of the forecourt and fountain before you go.
card.challenge: Catch a trolley or train sliding past behind the domes. Take a Live Photo, then pick your best frame afterwards.
card.good_to_know: Santa Fe Depot opened on 8 March 1915, just in time for the Panama–California Exposition. It replaced a small red-and-green Victorian depot from 1887. Today it's on the National Register of Historic Places and is a San Diego Historic Landmark.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand at the corner of Kettner Boulevard and Broadway, by the fountain in front of the depot. Face the building across the open forecourt for a low, street-level view with the fountain beside you.

selfie_spots.why: The plaza has tiled benches and a fountain, and one visitor photo was taken from it looking away from the depot toward America Plaza, which points the camera the right way for a selfie with the station behind.

card.hook: Picture a building that has a twin, and the twin is upside down in the water. That's the Botanical Building across the Lily Pond, and guides often call it the most photographed scene in Balboa Park.
card.stand_here: Stand at the pond's edge on the El Prado side and face north across the water to the Botanical Building. Its lath walls and roofline should mirror in the pond, with lilies and lotus floating in front of you.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to fit the building and its reflection together. Drop to zoom 0.5x if you're right at the water's edge and want more lilies in front, or try zoom 2x to pick out the lath roofline.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines and put the water's surface near the middle of the frame, so the building and its reflection get equal space.
card.best_time: Go early in the morning or at golden hour, on a calm day when the water is still and the reflection is at its best. Crouch a little or stand right at the edge so the plants sit low and the building fills the water behind them.
card.selfie_here: Stand at the front of the Botanical Building, facing out over the Lily Pond, so the building is behind you. It's a popular selfie spot. Use the front camera and try zoom 0.5x to squeeze more of the building in over your shoulder.
card.rules_and_safety: Check the official site before you go, both for whether the building is open and for any rules on photography inside.
card.challenge: Get a few lily pads low in the frame, then see if you can catch the water so still that people can't tell which building is the real one.
card.good_to_know: The pond view is outdoors on El Prado at 1549 El Prado, and it costs nothing to enjoy. Inside, light filters through the slatted roof onto tree ferns, orchids and palms. The building was under restoration from 2022 and reopened in winter 2024, so it's worth checking before you plan on going in.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand at the pond's edge on the El Prado side and face north across the water to the Botanical Building. Its lath walls and roofline should mirror in the pond, with lilies and lotus floating in front of you.

card.hook: Walk into Balboa Park and you'll spot a tall, slim tower with a blue-and-gold dome beside it, and you'll want a photo straight away. From the plaza it looks fairly small at first, so let the buildings do some of the work.
card.stand_here: Stand in Plaza de Panama, on the west side of the plaza, and look west along El Prado. The tower is about 3 minutes on foot to the west, and it sits to the left of the avenue.
card.zoom: Start at 1x to fit all of El Prado with the tower on the left. Then try 2x to bring the tower and dome closer. Use 0.5x only if you want lots of sky, and keep the tower away from the edge of the frame so it doesn't look stretched.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines, line the tower up with a vertical line so it stands tall and straight, then tap the tower and drag a little darker so the sky stays blue.
card.best_time: Morning is a good bet, because the sun is behind you as you look west and lights up the fronts of the buildings. In late afternoon the sun is more in front of you, so make the shot a little darker or step to one side.
card.selfie_here: Try the maze garden in Alcázar Garden: use the front camera, face away from the tower, and let the hedges and walkways frame you with the tower behind you. Cabrillo Bridge also works for a close selfie, with the tower and San Diego skyline behind you. Try 0.5x if you want more of it in the shot.
card.ask_someone: At Redwood Circle, ask a passer-by to stand back far enough to fit the whole tower in the frame while you pose with the tower behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: The tower's guided climb is paid, so check the official site for museum details and current access before you go.
card.challenge: Can you get all three tiers in one shot and name them: square, octagon, circle?
card.good_to_know: California Tower was built for the 1915–16 Panama–California Exposition and designed by Bertram Goodhue. It stands 198 feet (60 m) tall, and its three tiers change from a square to an octagon to a circle. The buildings now house the Museum of Us, and the carillon in the tower chimes every quarter-hour.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand in Plaza de Panama, on the west side of the plaza, and look west along El Prado. The tower is about 3 minutes on foot to the west, and it sits to the left of the avenue.

card.hook: This lighthouse had one big flaw: it sat so high on the cliff that fog and low cloud often hid it from the ships it was meant to guide. Today that same height gives you a bright white tower with a black cap, set against open sky.
card.stand_here: Stand at Old Point Loma Lighthouse, on the east-facing entrance side of the paved path that circles the building, and step back a few metres. Face the tower so the white walls and black lantern room fill the view, with the keeper's house beside it.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to fit the tower, the keeper's house and plenty of sky. Switch to 0.5x if you want the grounds and the picket fence in too, or try 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) to fill the frame with the black lantern room.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the white tower, then slide the brightness down a little (darker) so the white walls keep their detail and the sky stays blue.
card.best_time: Go in the morning for the east side, where the light is said to be cleanest and the lantern room sits against clear sky. In the afternoon the white picket fence throws nice shadows.
card.selfie_here: Try the front steps of the lighthouse, with the white tower behind you. Use the front camera, hold it at arm's length, and tilt it up a bit so the tower rises over your shoulder. This one comes from a portrait guide, so treat it as a good suggestion rather than a sure thing.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the paved path east of the tower, with the keeper's house on the left of their screen, so the whole lighthouse fits in behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: Photography is generally allowed inside the lighthouse, but follow any posted signs and skip the flash. The lighthouse is inside Cabrillo National Monument, which has an entry fee, so check the official site for current access and rules. Wind can be strong up here, so hold your phone with both hands.
card.challenge: Walk once around the paved path and take one shot from each side. Then pick the winner and see if it's the one with the fence shadows.
card.good_to_know: The lighthouse was built by the US government in 1855 and first lit at sunset on 15 November that year. It only shone until 1891, because a lower lighthouse replaced it once fog kept hiding it. In 1984 the National Park Service re-lit it for a celebration, the first time in 93 years, and it's now a museum.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand at Old Point Loma Lighthouse, on the east-facing entrance side of the paved path that circles the building, and step back a few metres. Face the tower so the white walls and black lantern room fill the view, with the keeper's house beside it.

card.hook: Picture a long, open walkway with a big curved stone stage waiting at the far end, like the park saved its best seat for last. That's the Spreckels Organ Pavilion, and it has more than 5,000 organ pipes behind those arches.
card.stand_here: Stand on the north side of Plaza de Panama and face south, looking down the long approach to the pavilion. Confirm the exact spot when you arrive, because the whole structure should sit framed at the end with the organ building behind it.
card.zoom: Start at 1x to fit the whole colonnade in from the plaza. Walk closer and switch to 0.5x for the full curve of the facade. Use 2x or more (it depends on your phone) for close-ups of the arches, pillars and gables.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and put the middle of the colonnade on the centre line so the symmetry looks neat, then tap the colonnade and drag it a bit darker if the sky is washing out the stone.
card.best_time: Pick a quieter day instead of Sunday around 2 pm, when the free concert crowds can block the front view. Late-afternoon light can look lovely through the archways, though that may not hold at every time of year.
card.selfie_here: Sit on one of the benches in front of the pavilion so the whole curved structure fills the background behind you. For another look, stand between the columns or near the steps on the pavilion's sides, where the pillars and arches frame you. Use the front camera, and try 0.5x to fit more of the curve in.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand in the open area out front so they can capture the whole bowl, while you walk toward the pavilion with the curved colonnade behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: The seating faces south straight into the San Diego sun, so bring a hat, sunscreen, water and maybe an umbrella for shade. It's an open-air venue in a public park, but events can change what you can access, so check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Take one shot with the colonnade perfectly centred, then one close-up of an arch. Can you tell the two apart from a friend's across-the-room glance? (They should look like two different places.)
card.good_to_know: The pavilion was built for the 1915 Panama–California Exposition in an Italian-Renaissance style. John D. Spreckels and his brother Adolph gave it and the organ to the people of San Diego on 31 December 1914. The organ is described as the world's largest pipe organ in a fully outdoor venue.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on the north side of Plaza de Panama and face south, looking down the long approach to the pavilion. Confirm the exact spot when you arrive, because the whole structure should sit framed at the end with the organ building behind it.

card.hook: Plot twist: you can't walk out on Ocean Beach Pier right now, and that's fine, because the best photo is from down on the rocks looking up at it.
card.stand_here: Stand about 950 m south-east of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face north-west. That puts you at the Ocean Beach Tidepools at the foot of Newport Avenue, right below the pier.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x and hold the phone low for a close view of the pier's supports. Use zoom 1x for the pier and surf from the shore end, and zoom 2x-5x (depends on your phone) for pelicans and gulls.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the pier or the nearest rock, then drag the slider a little darker so the sky doesn't wash out.
card.best_time: Go at low tide, when the tidepool area is at its best, and check the tide times before you set out. Golden hour is a lovely time for the pier's pilings too.
card.selfie_here: Try the dry sand at the landward foot of the pier, between the concrete pilings. Use the front camera at zoom 0.5x and hold your arm out so the pier sits over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the beach looking northwest toward the pier, while you stand on the sand between them and the pier so the whole structure is behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: The pier itself is closed to the public, so check the City of San Diego site for its current status. Be careful on the slippery tidepool rocks, and don't turn your back to the ocean. Personal photos are generally fine, but be mindful of privacy when other people are in your shot.
card.challenge: Get a pelican or gull in the foreground with the pier's supports leading out to sea behind it. Bonus points if a surfer sneaks in too.
card.good_to_know: The pier has been closed since storm damage, and the City of San Diego is planning a long-term replacement. Ocean Beach has had that name since 1887. Surfing was introduced to San Diego here in 1916, so a surfer in your frame suits the place.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand about 950 m south-east of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face north-west. That puts you at the Ocean Beach Tidepools at the foot of Newport Avenue, right below the pier.

card.hook: Halfway across Cabrillo Bridge, you can look over the railing and watch the highway sliding by far below you. It's a bit of a thrill, and the skyline out front makes it a great photo.
card.stand_here: Stand on Cabrillo Bridge at the centre of the span, on the footway. Face out over the deck and railings towards the Downtown San Diego skyline, with Balboa Park's gardens and buildings beyond.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to take in the bridge. Then try zoom 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) to pick out the arches and the deck. On the span itself, zoom 0.5x fits the deck, railings and skyline into one shot.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines, put the railing along the lower third, tap the skyline, and at sunset drag the brighter/darker slider down a little so the sky keeps its colour.
card.best_time: Sunset gives a warm golden glow over the city and the bridge. Early morning is calmer, because weekends and event days are the busiest.
card.selfie_here: Head down to the dirt trail in Cabrillo Canyon, at the base of the bridge's west side. Use the front camera, hold it a little low, and let the arches rise behind you. If you can't fit them in, switch to 0.5x.
card.ask_someone: Ask your passer-by to stand farther back on the canyon trail, where the whole bridge and its arches fit in the frame, while you stand at the base of the bridge.
card.rules_and_safety: The footway is shared with a two-lane road, so keep your feet on the pavement and out of traffic when you step back for a shot. The canyon trail is unpaved with some descent and may be steep or muddy. The bridge has been closed for works before, so check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Can you count all seven arches in one photo without cutting any off?
card.good_to_know: Cabrillo Bridge was built for the Panama–California Exposition of 1915. It was the first multiple-arched cantilever bridge in California. It has seven arches on fourteen hollow concrete pillars, and the main span stands 120 feet (37 m) above the canyon floor. With its approaches, it's about 279 m long.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on Cabrillo Bridge at the centre of the span, on the footway. Face out over the deck and railings towards the Downtown San Diego skyline, with Balboa Park's gardens and buildings beyond.
